Afrinext · phase 4 · marketplace & universal store engine

One Table, Six Trades, and Nothing Invented

A formation academy, a tailor, a courier and a photographer now open a shop through the same schema, the same authorization and the same discovery queries — differing only in the words on screen. And the marketplace that lists them shows no rating, no follower count, no verification badge and no sales figure, because Afrinext has none of those facts and a buyer in Niamey is the wrong person to show an invented number to.

What this milestone is, in one paragraph

The product side of Afrinext was a fake-data prototype: seeded listings, invented star ratings, a "saved" list in localStorage. All of it is deleted. In its place is a store engine — one stores table with a validated store_type, a lifecycle with a moderation path, visibility decided in SQL, and a marketplace that reads only facts the database actually holds.

No money moved and no ledger row was written. Settlement, payouts, refund execution and the payment state machine are untouched — see section H.

A

Six businesses, one entity, and why that is not a shortcut

The brief named six things Afrinext must sell: formations, digital products, physical products, services, creator work and delivery. The tempting reading is six features. It is one.

A training academy in Niamey and a mechanic on the Route de Tillabéri need the same things from a marketplace: an identity buyers can find, a list of what they offer, a price in XOF, an owner who controls it, and a moderator who can stop it. What differs is vocabulary and presentation — "formations" versus "prestations" — not structure.

Six near-identical tables would have to be kept in step forever. Every feature after this one — moderation, search, commission, payouts, suspension — would be written six times, and the sixth copy would be the one with the bug. So the type is a column, and the differences live in a presentation layer that cannot reach a query.

There is no default type, and that is a product decision

parseStoreType throws for anything not on the list — including undefined, "", "FORMATION" and "service ". It never falls back.

The type decides how somebody's shop presents itself to buyers. Guessing it means guessing their business. A seller who does not answer the question does not get a store, and the wizard's first step cannot be skipped: the Continue button is disabled until one of the six is chosen.

B

Lifecycle, ownership, and three guards that live in SQL

TransitionWhoPermissionNote
→ draftthe creatorstore.createowner is the session, never the input
draft → publishedownerstore.updatestamps published_at once
published → draftownerstore.updateunpublishStore
any → suspendedmoderatorstore.moderatereason of ≥4 characters, audited
suspended → draftmoderatorstore.moderatenot to published
suspended → publishednobody—the SQL excludes it

Three of these carry a reason worth stating.

Republishing cannot jump the queue

published_at = coalesce(published_at, now()),
-- not now(): the first publish stamps it and later ones leave it alone

"Newest stores" is the most valuable position on the marketplace home. With a bare now(), a seller could hold it indefinitely by unpublishing and republishing every morning. The coalesce is what makes that date mean when this store first became public.

Reinstatement returns a store to draft, not to published

Lifting a suspension restores the owner's ability to be public; it does not publish on their behalf. A seller whose store was suspended over a disputed listing should decide when it goes back up — not discover that a moderator did it for them, with the old listing still on it.

The guards are in the statement, not before it

update stores set status = 'published', ...
 where id = $1 and status <> 'suspended'

store_type = case when status = 'draft' then coalesce($1, store_type)
                  else store_type end

A read followed by a check leaves a gap: a suspension landing between the two would be overwritten by a publish that had already decided the store was fine. Putting both conditions inside the UPDATE closes it — the row either matches or the statement affects nothing, and the caller is told so.

The second is why a published store's kind cannot change. Buyers have seen it presented one way and its offerings were written for that presentation. Turning a formation into a delivery service is not an edit; it is a different business.

Ownership comes from the session and from nowhere else

owner_user_id is actor.userId. There is no field in any request through which somebody could open a store in another person's name — and a test posts ownerUserId, owner_user_id and userId together, all naming a second seller, to prove the row still belongs to the sender. store.moderate is deliberately a platform permission: owning a store is not it, so a seller cannot suspend a rival, or themselves.

C

Visibility is decided in SQL, or it is not decided

Every public query filters status = 'published' in the statement. A draft store is not a row the caller receives and declines to render. It is a row the caller never receives.

FunctionFilter
findPublicStoreslug = $1 and status = 'published'
listPublicProductsp.status = 'published' and s.status = 'published'
discoverStoress.status = 'published'
discoverOfferingsp.status = 'published' and s.status = 'published'
countStoresByTypestatus = 'published'

Both conditions on the offering queries, always. A published product inside a suspended store is not public, and the join enforces that rather than trusting a caller to check the store separately. The browser test proves it from outside: it publishes a store, publishes a product in it, confirms both are reachable anonymously, suspends the store, and then asserts the product is gone from discovery too.

"Not published" and "does not exist" are the same answer

findPublicStore returns undefined for a draft store, a suspended store and a slug nobody ever took. The route turns all three into a 404. Telling them apart would let a stranger enumerate which slugs are in use and which sellers have been suspended.

The public projection is not a cast

PublicStore is built field by field from StoreRecord, which carries the owner's user id and the internal store id. Naming the ten public fields is what stops a column added next year — an internal note, a moderation flag, a risk score — from reaching a stranger's browser because somebody ran a migration. Mutation S5 replaces the projection with a cast; a test fails.

D

A defect the type system introduced, and the fix

This one is worth reading in full, because the cause was the opposite of careless.

CreateStoreInput.storeType was typed StoreType — the strictest thing available. That forced every HTTP boundary to call parseStoreType to satisfy the compiler, which put input validation before authorization:

// before — the compiler required this, and this is the bug
await catalog.createStore(db, actor, {
  storeType: catalog.parseStoreType(body.storeType),  // throws first
  ...
});                                                   // authorize() never reached

A stranger posting to POST /api/v1/stores was answered 400 "unsupported store type" instead of 403 "denied" — a fact about the API's shape that they had not earned. The browser suite caught it: three consent tests and one catalog test went red the moment storeType became required, all reporting 400 where they expected 403 or 451.

The fix is to type the field raw and let the domain parse it, after both gates:

Reviewer's note — the type annotation is deliberately weaker

storeType: StoreType | (string & {}) looks like a loosening and reads like a mistake. It is neither. The comment at the field says why, and mutation S11 — which moves the parse back above the gates — is killed by two tests. The value is still validated; it is validated in the one place that can be sure the gates have already run.

E

Nothing on this marketplace is invented

The brief was explicit, and so is the code. There is no rating, no review count, no follower total, no "verified" badge, no seeded featured flag, no view counter and no random ordering anywhere in marketplace.ts or in the interface that reads it.

Two facts are real, and those are the two shown: when a store was published, and how many published offerings it has — including zero, said plainly as "Aucune offre pour l'instant".

SortOrderingWhat it reads
newest (default)published_at desc nulls lasta real timestamp
popularcount(paid orders) desc, published_at descorders.status = 'paid', nothing else

A pending checkout, an expired one and a failed one are not sales. Counting them would measure interest and call it demand — so the test inserts three of exactly those against one store, asserts the ranking does not move, then adds a single paid order to the other store and asserts it now outranks all three.

The row that is not shown

The marketplace home does not render the "popular" row at all until it would differ from the newest row. With no sales, "popular" is recency wearing a different label, and presenting it that way is precisely the fabrication this section exists to avoid. The screenshots in section F were taken against a database with no paid orders, which is why that row is absent from them.

The counts on the category tiles

Mutation S6 made countStoresByType include drafts and suspensions, and no test failed. That was a real gap: the home page's category tiles would have advertised a marketplace larger than the one that exists, every extra being a shop nobody can open — the same fabrication as a fake rating, arriving through arithmetic. A test now creates one live creator store, one draft and one suspended, and requires the count to be 1.

Search, and its bound

ILIKE over name, tagline and description: the honest tool for a marketplace with tens of stores — nothing extra to run, nothing to keep warm, predictable in French. The pattern is escaped, so a buyer searching for 100% gets that string rather than a wildcard; the test names one store "Promo 100% coton" and requires that search to return exactly it and not the other. limit is clamped to 1–48 and offset to 0–5000, so no URL asks for the whole marketplace at once.

F

The interface, as it actually renders

Every screenshot below is a real page from a production build, served by next start against PostgreSQL. All four widths — 390, 768, 1280 and 1680 — were inspected, and a script asserts zero horizontal overflow at every one of them on every page shown.

The marketplace

Each card carries a brand-washed cover, the store's monogram, its type and its real offering count. The six palettes — laterite, indigo, forest, ochre, aubergine, sable — are named for materials rather than hex values, and a store that chooses none gets one deterministically from its slug, so a shop is never unstyled and always looks the same.

African identity through restraint

The brief warned against tribal decoration, random flags and stereotype. What is here instead: a palette taken from laterite earth, indigo dye, harmattan ochre and sahel green; a diagonal weave in the covers at low opacity, reading as woven cloth rather than as a pattern library; generous type; French first, because the launch market is Niger. No mask, no map of Africa, no kente border.

Opening a store: four questions, not nine fields

A single form with nine fields tells a first-time seller in Niamey that this will be hard. Four short screens with one question each tell them it will not. Nothing is submitted until the last step, so abandoning the flow leaves no half-built store behind — and the client state is a nicer way to fill a form, never a security boundary: the server validates every field again.

The seller's dashboard tells them what to do next

Publishing is offered only when there is something to publish

The dashboard withholds "Publier la boutique" until the store has at least one offering. Nobody is invited to publish an empty shop that a buyer would then land on. The browser test asserts the button is absent at that point, adds a product, and then finds it.

Search and browse, with no client JavaScript at all

Query, type, sort and page all live in URL search params. A result is therefore a link somebody can send to a friend, the back button steps through searches, and the whole screen renders on the server. That is not a purity exercise: this is a marketplace for phones on mobile data, and the fastest search result is one that arrives as HTML.

One survivor, found and closed

S6 made countStoresByType count drafts and suspensions, and the whole suite stayed green. The category tiles on the marketplace home would have advertised stores no visitor can reach.

This is the same failure mode the profile and channel milestones each hit once, and it is worth naming again: the tests all approached that function through the marketplace pages, where only published stores exist anyway. A count that included drafts produced the same number in every test that had ever been written. The fix is not a stricter assertion on an existing test but a test that creates the states nothing else creates — one live store, one draft, one suspended, of the same type — and demands the count be 1. S6 is killed on re-run.

H

The financial boundary, results, and what is not built

No money moved

Explicitly not implemented and not started, as the milestone required: settlement, payouts, seller withdrawals, wallet movements, commission payment, referral payout, refund execution, payment capture logic, and any ledger posting.

The only money this milestone reads is orders.status = 'paid', counted for ranking. It writes nothing to orders, payments, ledger_entries, account_balances or refunds. The payment state machine approved in phase 3 is untouched, and the OTP and authentication paths were not modified. Ledger reconciliation over a full capture → settlement → payout cycle is clean: 0 drift, 0 unbalanced transactions, net 0 XOF.

9d5d1cf is dffae04 plus this note itself; CI ran on it and all three jobs — dependency scan, lint · typecheck · test, and the browser assertions — passed. The code under review is dffae04.

The 16 skipped tests are the iPayMoney sandbox integration suite, gated on credentials that are not present in this environment. They are unchanged.

Three defects this milestone found in work that was already green

  1. Twenty test fixtures inserted published stores with no publication date

    The new stores_published_has_timestamp CHECK rejected them, in three e2e specs and the reconciliation probe. They had always been wrong — a published store with a null published_at sorts last forever — but nothing had ever asked.

  2. A silent role grant in a test helper

    insert … select … from roles where key = $1 grants nothing when the key does not exist, and says so silently. A misspelled role produced an actor with no permissions, so every test asserting a refusal would have passed for entirely the wrong reason. The helper now checks the row count and throws.

  3. A seller with no permission was invited into a wizard that would refuse them

    The redesigned /fr/sell lost the "not yet a seller" state and offered everybody the create-store button. Both the screen and the route now check store.create — and the browser test types the wizard's URL directly to prove the route check is the one that matters.

What is deliberately not built

ExtensionWhere it landsStatus
Course structureproducts.kind = 'course' + course_moduleslater milestone
Physical goodskind = 'physical' + stock, weight, delivery zonelater milestone
Serviceskind = 'service' + availability, call-out radiuslater milestone
Delivery jobsa job table keyed on the storelater milestone
Settlement, payouts, refundsthe ledger, already builtnot started, by instruction

products is digital-only today (kind = 'digital', enforced by a CHECK) and the engine does not pretend otherwise: a physical-product store can be created, published and found, and selling a physical item needs the product side extended. Each extension above is a new kind plus a table referencing products, behind the same authorization, the same publication rules and the same discovery queries. Nothing in this milestone has to be revisited to add one.

Open questions for the reviewer

  1. Is "publish requires an offering" the right rule?

    It prevents a buyer landing on an empty shop, but it also means a seller cannot claim a slug and a public page before they have stock. The alternative is to allow publishing an empty store and show the honest "Aucune offre" state — which the marketplace card already renders. Say which you prefer; it is one condition.

  2. Slug collisions are refused, not resolved.

    A second "Atelier Couture" is told the address is taken rather than being given atelier-couture-2, which is not a name anybody chose. That is a judgement, and it is reversible in one function.

  3. The seller role is still granted by SQL.

    There is no admin console yet, so becoming a seller is an operator running an INSERT. Unchanged from the previous milestone and called out again because it is the one gap in an otherwise complete seller journey.
